reader.title: Hanging of an army recruit at Gardiner, Montana
bases: A few men hanged an accused thief by the neck from a beam, without legal authority, until he confessed, leaving him 'more dead than alive'; he survived (A2, A3).

The recruit survived and was handed to his commanding officer (A2, A3), so no one was killed; the men acted without authority to punish and extract a confession from an accused thief, and 'a few determined men' gives no exact number (A2, A3).

The Livingston Enterprise (A1, A2) and the separately worded Livingston dispatch in the River Press (A3) agree on the theft at Mrs. Metcalf's house, the hanging to force a confession and the handover to Captain Harris; later items are reprints or condensations.

summary.text: The hanging of an army recruit at Gardiner, Montana, took place on August 29, 1888, when a few men put a noose around the neck of an unnamed soldier accused of stealing from the house of a woman who had just died and hanged him from a beam until he told where he had hidden the goods.
He survived and was handed over to his commanding officer, Captain Harris, "more dead than alive."

Montana papers presented the episode as the climax of misconduct by a "tough" batch of sixteen recruits, and a condensed version circulated as a filler paragraph in papers from Texas to Virginia into December 1888.

According to the Livingston Enterprise, the sixteen soldiers had been sent as a reinforcement to Captain Harris at the Mammoth Hot Springs, and most had been involved in crime and disobedience since they arrived.

A Livingston dispatch printed in the River Press said they had come from Fort Keogh, that six were in the guard house and three had deserted, and that one had been sent back to Fort Keogh to be court-martialed.
Shortly before the hanging, another recruit tried to take over the hotel at the springs, insulted Lieutenant Tutherly when ordered back to camp, and was marched to the guard house at pistol point.
On Wednesday, August 29, one of the recruits went to Gardiner and, told that Mrs. Metcalf had died, asked to see her remains and was let into the house.
After he left, a satchel, a gold watch and some money were missed; the Enterprise called the satchel a valise and also listed some gold dust.
People from the house searched for him and found him, but he denied knowing where the things were.
A few men, "confident that he was the guilty party," then got a rope, put it around his neck and swung him from a nearby beam.
It took "several severe jerks" before he confessed and told where the goods were hidden, and they were recovered.
The men then turned him over to Captain Harris for military discipline.
No account names the recruit or the men who hanged him, and no report of an arrest or charge against them appears in the coverage.
What military discipline the recruit received is not reported.
According to the River Press dispatch, regrets were "freely expressed" that he had not been hanged to death.

The Livingston Enterprise reported the hanging on September 1 as the end of its account of the "famous squad," describing the recruit as "devoid of the slightest feelings of manhood" and handing him over to "the tender mercies of Captain Harris."
The Fort Benton River Press ran the Livingston dispatch on September 5 under the headline "A Tough Lot," with its closing remark about regrets that the recruit had survived.
Nearly the same text appeared on September 6 in the Emporia Weekly News, under a Helena dateline of September 4, and in the Reporter and Farmer of Webster, Dakota.

From October a shortened paragraph beginning "Army recruits are not of first quality nowadays" ran in the Waco Evening News and in Dakota weeklies, among them the Reporter and Farmer and the Wahpeton Times.

The same paragraph reached the Emmons County Record, the Hot Springs Star and the Sully County Watchman in October and November, and the Iuka Reporter in Mississippi and the Clinch Valley News in Virginia in mid-December.

This version placed the recruits at Livingston, said one had gone to Fort Benton for court-martial, dropped Gardiner and Mrs. Metcalf, and said the thief had been "strung up by indignant citizens"; the December printings read "a dead women."
In the filler the hanging was one example in an item about the poor quality of army recruits rather than a report of mob violence.
The two local accounts differ only on the stolen goods, a valise with gold dust in the Enterprise and a satchel without it in the River Press.

accounts.label: Livingston Enterprise (local weekly)
accounts.gist: A recruit admitted to Mrs. Metcalf's house left with a valise, gold watch, money and gold dust; a few men, sure of his guilt, swung him from a beam until he confessed, and the goods were recovered.

accounts.label: Livingston dispatch (River Press)
accounts.gist: Same sequence, with a satchel, gold watch and money; he was hanged until he confessed and handed to Captain Harris 'more dead than alive', with regrets that he was not hanged to death.

accounts.label: Condensed filler paragraph
accounts.gist: One of sixteen recruits at Livingston 'was strung up by indignant citizens' and made to confess where he hid goods stolen from a dead woman.

framing.detail: The Livingston Enterprise called the recruits a 'famous squad' and described the victim as 'devoid of the slightest feelings of manhood', handing him to 'the tender mercies of Captain Harris'.
The River Press headlined it 'A Tough Lot' and reported regrets that he was not hanged to the finish of his 'miserable life'.
Distant papers ran the condensed paragraph 'Army recruits are not of first quality' as filler about bad recruits, not as news of mob violence.
